When certainty is low, our confidence in the estimated effect is limited, and the true effect may vary substantially from the estimate. 3. In cases of very low certainty, we have minimal confidence in the estimated effect, and the true effect is likely to differ significantly from the estimate. 4. Healthcare providers (HCPs) and Village Health Workers (VHVs) are key stakeholders in implementing health interventions. 5. The evidence was downgraded by two levels due to significant concerns about bias, including unclear random sequence generation, lack of allocation concealment, and the inability to blind participants due to the nature of the intervention. Additionally, there were issues with incomplete outcome reporting and unclear blinding of outcomes. 6. The evidence was downgraded by one level due to imprecision, which was attributed to small sample sizes and limited reporting. 7. Mobile phone-based interventions have been shown to improve hepatitis B birth dose vaccination rates in rural areas, as demonstrated in studies like Xeuavongsa et al. (2016). 8. Studies often had varying numbers of respondents at different follow-up times, depending on the participant group (e.g., HCPs, VHVs, women/parents). No meta-analyses were conducted in these studies. 9. Notification of births and deaths using mobile phones, either alone or in combination with other strategies, may enhance accountability among providers and health systems for collecting vital data and delivering post-notification services. 10. Local capacity for training future notifiers can be strengthened through train-the-trainer approaches, as highlighted in studies like Ngabo (2012) and MBRL (2011). 11. Continuous monitoring and supportive supervision mechanisms are critical for ensuring the quality and timeliness of birth and death data collected via mobile devices. 12. The implementation of mobile-based birth and death notification systems may be influenced by the underlying health and civil registration infrastructure, resources, and processes. 13. Costs incurred by healthcare providers for sending notifications using personal mobile phones may need reimbursement to ensure sustained use of these technologies. 14. Mobile phone-based notification systems are generally acceptable to healthcare providers and are perceived as supportive of their job responsibilities. 15. Rigorous training on the use of mobile devices, along with post-training support, may be necessary for notifiers who lack prior experience or familiarity with mobile technologies. 16. Competing priorities and insufficient incentives may hinder the successful adoption of mobile notification strategies by healthcare providers. 17. For some families, financial barriers may prevent the completion of birth and death registration processes after notification. 18. Targeted demand-generation activities in communities with low awareness of the importance of birth and death registration may be necessary alongside mobile notification interventions. 19. Socio-cultural norms can influence the timely identification of births and deaths and should be considered when designing mobile phone-based notification interventions. 20. Strong government commitment has been identified as a key factor in the successful implementation of mobile-based birth and death notification systems. 21. The cost of purchasing, setting up, and scaling mobile technologies for birth and death notification is an important consideration, as reported by several studies. 22. Network connectivity availability is a critical factor for the successful implementation and scaling of mobile-based notification systems. 23. Data security and encryption measures vary across studies, but they are essential for maintaining the confidentiality of birth and death information transmitted via mobile devices. 24. While mobile-based notification systems aim to reach under-registered populations, inequities in implementation have been reported, often related to infrastructure, human factors (e.g., age, gender, literacy, poverty), and donor funding priorities. 25. The World Health Organization (WHO) has initiated guidelines to inform government-led investments in digital health strategies, particularly for strengthening reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health (RMNCAH) interventions. 26. Systematic reviews commissioned by WHO aim to explore factors influencing the acceptability, feasibility, and implementation of telemedicine interventions, with a focus on mobile-based technologies. 27. Telemedicine is defined as the provision of healthcare services at a distance, involving communication between healthcare providers or between remote users and providers. 28. Interactive telemedicine, where inquiries receive real-time or clinically appropriate responses, is the primary focus of these reviews. 29. Reviews included in the analysis adhered to systematic methodologies, including clear objectives, reproducible methods, systematic searches, and assessments of study validity. 30. Data extraction and thematic analysis were conducted to synthesize findings, and confidence in the results was assessed using an adapted GRADE-CERQual approach.
